passage:
Jasleen scrolled through the openings at the three firms she liked and noticed what recruiters asked for: working with messy data, and getting something live. So instead of ten tutorial copies she picked two projects, one cleaning and analysing bus-delay records, the other a small app that she put online.

Before touching code, she sketched the site on paper: a home page, a page for each project, a contact corner. Beside each project she wrote four boxes: the problem, her part, the result, a link.

Zubin, in her class, started a portfolio the same month. He changed the font on Monday, the animation on Wednesday and the colours on Friday, and did the same again the next week. Two months later the site was still on his laptop, and no recruiter had seen a single page.

Jasleen published hers. A senior, Dhruv, looked it over. "You list the tools," he said, "but what changed?" She rewrote each project in three lines: the problem, what she built, and what got better, such as how the search for bus delays dropped from an hour to five minutes.

qa.q: How many projects did Jasleen choose?
qa.a: Jasleen chose two projects.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen's portfolio reach recruiters while Zubin's did not?
qa.a: Jasleen picked projects that recruiters wanted, sketched the pages and published, then improved the site after Dhruv's comment, while Zubin kept changing fonts and animations and never put the site online.

qa.q: What was Jasleen probably feeling when Dhruv asked what changed?
qa.a: Probably a little exposed but open to it, since she rewrote each project straight away.

qa.q: What could Zubin do this week?
qa.a: Zubin could publish the current version, then improve it in small steps with comments from a peer or senior.

grounding: Four approaches to building a portfolio: working backward from employers, sketching the site, delaying launch for perfection, and asking others to critique it.

passage:
At the festival market, Ira let go of her mother's sari for one second, and the crowd carried them apart. Her heart pounded. Then she remembered the rule: if you get lost, stop moving. Ira stood by a bangle stall, reasoning that Mama would walk back along the way they had come. Three minutes later, Dolma's voice came through the crowd, calling her name.

Before entering the bazaar that morning, Rehan's mother Hansa had asked, "What will you do if we get separated?" Rehan said it aloud twice: stop, find a shop, say Papa's number, don't leave the area.

But at the spice lane the crowd swallowed Rehan's family, and his mind went blank. When a smiling man said, "I know where your mother is, come," Rehan followed without asking a thing. After ten minutes he was two lanes from the meeting spot, and the man had gone quiet and vague.

Rehan stopped beside a chai stall. The rehearsed words came back. "Uncle, please call my father," he said, and read out the number. The owner rang, and Papa arrived, red-faced and relieved, within minutes.

qa.q: Where did Ira stand after being separated?
qa.a: Ira stood by a bangle stall.

qa.q: How did Rehan's choices differ from Ira's, and what happened to each?
qa.a: Ira stopped moving and waited, and her mother found her within minutes, while Rehan followed a stranger, ended up two lanes from the meeting spot, and got help only after he stopped and asked the chai stall owner.

qa.q: What was Rehan feeling in the spice lane?
qa.a: Panic: his mind went blank and he followed the first man who offered help.

qa.q: What could Rehan do if a stranger offers to take him to his mother?
qa.a: Rehan could say no thank you, stay where he is, and ask a shop owner or another trusted adult to phone home.

grounding: Four approaches to being lost in a crowded market: staying put, rehearsing a plan, following a stranger, and switching to staying and asking.

passage:
Three toddlers on Ashok Lane hit small problems one afternoon.

Divyansh's toy car stopped making its noise. He scooped it up, toddled across the room to his father, held it high and said, "No." His father took the car and pressed the button until it whirred.

Afreen had heard her mother call "Dadi!" whenever a cup broke. Now her shoe strap flopped open. She looked at it, turned toward the next room and shouted, "Dadi!" Footsteps came at once.

Jagdish's teddy had slipped down behind the sofa. He stood over the gap and screamed. His mother heard the noise from the kitchen but could not tell what was wrong, and by the time she came, Jagdish's face was red and wet. Later that week the teddy went behind the sofa again. "Wait a minute," said his mother, stirring a pot. Jagdish gripped her finger, pulled her across the room and jabbed at the gap. "Ted," he said. She reached in and pulled the teddy out.

qa.q: Who did Divyansh carry his car to?
qa.a: Divyansh carried the car to his father.

qa.q: Why did help arrive late for Jagdish the first time but quickly the second time?
qa.a: The first time Jagdish only screamed from the spot, so his mother could not tell what was wrong; the second time he pulled her by the finger to the sofa and jabbed at the gap, so the problem was shown.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he stood over the gap the first time?
qa.a: Frustration and distress: he screamed and his face was red and wet.

qa.q: How could Jagdish's mother help him keep asking this way?
qa.a: She could go to him when he calls, name the problem, and welcome it when he leads her by the hand.

grounding: Four toddler approaches to fetching help: using the caregiver as a tool, imitating a call for help, screaming from the spot, and leading the caregiver to the problem.

passage:
The scooter skidded on loose gravel and the rider, Pradeep, lay in the road by the bend. Pranav, on his bike, pulled over well off the tarmac, switched on his hazard lights, looked up the road for oncoming traffic, and only then called the emergency number for an ambulance and the police. In his head ran the steps from a first-aid class: check safety, get help coming, leave a badly hurt person where they are unless the spot is dangerous, and tell only what you know. He gave the operator the place and what he saw, with no guesses.

Beside him, Madhav had jumped off a bus and lifted his phone to record. Madhav stood there filming while Pradeep lay waiting. Nobody had called anyone. Only when Pranav said, "Have you called?" did Madhav lower the phone and dial with him.

Days later Pranav still heard the brakes at night and could not settle. He talked it over with his family and saw a doctor about the sleepless nights. He also made new rules for himself: helmet every ride, slower on bends, no night rides on that road.

qa.q: What did Pranav do before calling the emergency number?
qa.a: He pulled over off the tarmac, switched on his hazard lights, and looked up the road for oncoming traffic.

qa.q: How did Madhav's response differ from Pranav's, and what did that mean for Pradeep?
qa.a: Pranav made himself safe and called for help at once, while Madhav filmed and nobody called, so Pradeep waited longer for trained help.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling in the days after the crash?
qa.a: Shaken and unsettled: he still heard the brakes at night and could not settle.

qa.q: What could a bystander do if they freeze?
qa.a: They could take a breath and go through simple steps: check safety, ask someone to call, and stay near the injured person.

grounding: Four approaches to a road accident: safety and emergency call, a learned checklist, filming instead of helping, and support and new habits afterwards.

passage:
Indu sat her doll on the sofa arm and whispered the game to it. "You are sick. I listen to your chest. Then I give medicine." She tapped the doll's chest twice, then held out an empty spoon.

Later, on the mat, Indu and Uday settled roles: Indu the doctor, Uday the parent. They fetched a toy stethoscope, a bandage and a rug for the clinic before anyone said a word of the story.

At the other end of the room, Varun was playing shop with Tara. "No, you say 'how much?' first," Varun said. "No, not like that." After the fifth correction Tara put the basket down and wandered off to the book corner.

Back at the clinic, the game slowed after the check-up. Uday yawned and looked at the ceiling. Indu jumped up. "Emergency! The baby has a fever!" Uday dashed for the doll, and the clinic was busy again.

qa.q: What did Indu say to the doll?
qa.a: She said, "You are sick. I listen to your chest. Then I give medicine."

qa.q: Why did Indu and Uday's game last while Varun and Tara's ended?
qa.a: Indu and Uday settled roles, fetched a stethoscope and bandage, and Indu shouted about an emergency when the game slowed, while Varun kept saying no to Tara until Tara wandered off after the fifth correction.

qa.q: What was Tara probably feeling after the fifth correction?
qa.a: Fed up and bored, because the game no longer felt like hers.

qa.q: What could Varun try instead?
qa.a: Varun could let Tara make up some of her own lines and add a twist, so the game can go new ways.

grounding: Four approaches to planning a pretend game: talking it through beforehand, setting up roles and props, holding to rigid rules, and adding a problem to the story.

passage:
Trisha's first salary was Rs 30,000. Before she bought anything, she wrote down what was not optional: rent, food, transport, the phone bill. Adding them up, she stared at the remainder, which was far smaller than the bank alert had suggested. On salary day she also set up an automatic transfer of a fixed sum into a separate account and a small monthly investment, so that saving happened before spending.

Tushar, two desks away, saw the same credit and felt rich. He bought a phone on monthly instalments, ordered dinner most nights and treated friends. By the twentieth his account was empty, and he borrowed lunch money from Lokesh, who had watched it coming.

Tushar was embarrassed, but Lokesh said only, "Where did it go?" The next month Tushar noted each payment made on his phone. On the last day he counted: food delivery was the largest slice. He set a weekly limit for it and stuck a reminder on his screen.

qa.q: How much was Trisha's first salary?
qa.a: Trisha's first salary was Rs 30,000.

qa.q: Why did Tushar's month go differently from Trisha's, and what did he change?
qa.a: Trisha totalled her fixed costs and set up automatic saving before spending, while Tushar treated the credit as plenty and had nothing left by the twentieth; only after noting every payment for a month did he find food delivery and cap it.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he borrowed lunch money?
qa.a: Embarrassed, though Lokesh's simple question helped him look at what had happened.

qa.q: What could Tushar do next?
qa.a: Tushar could keep noting his payments and keep the weekly limit, and ask someone he trusts, like Trisha, how she plans her month.

grounding: Four approaches to a first salary: fixed costs first, saving automatically, spending freely, and tracking real spending before setting limits.
